title: The Invisible Handshake: Why API Contracts Matter More Than Code Reviews
excerpt: Code reviews catch bugs, but broken API contracts ship silently to production and break everything downstream.

content.text: I once spent three hours debugging a Flutter app that was crashing on startup, only to discover the backend had renamed a single JSON field from "user_id" to "userId" without telling anyone. The app compiled fine, the tests passed, and the crash only happened in production for real users. No code review in the world would have caught that — it was a contract violation, not a code defect.

When you build a mobile app with Flutter and Supabase, or a Chrome extension like SyncMind that talks to multiple AI provider APIs, you are essentially writing code that depends on promises made by other systems. Those promises — the shape of your JSON, the status codes you return, the headers you accept — are your API contracts. And unlike application code, they are rarely reviewed with the same rigor.

In my experience, the most insidious bugs come not from what you write, but from what you assume. When Bolo AI sends a voice query to Gemini API, it assumes the response will contain certain fields. When Career Verse fetches career recommendations from a FastAPI backend, it assumes the payload structure hasn't changed. These assumptions are rarely documented, rarely tested, and almost never reviewed.
An undocumented API is a broken API waiting to happen.
content.author: Roshan Lal Yogi

content.text: The solution isn't more code reviews — it's making contracts first-class citizens of your development process. Start with a shared schema file, whether that's a JSON Schema, an OpenAPI spec, or even a TypeScript interface that both frontend and backend agree on. Treat changes to that schema with the same scrutiny you give a database migration.

In practice, this means when I build a Next.js dashboard that consumes a FastAPI service, I generate types from the OpenAPI spec and commit to never hand-writing API response shapes. When I extend SyncMind to support a new AI provider, I define the expected request and response formats before writing a single line of adapter code. The contract becomes the source of truth, not the implementation.

This approach has saved me countless hours. Instead of chasing phantom bugs in production, I catch contract mismatches at build time. Instead of debugging why a Flutter widget isn't rendering data, I see immediately that the backend changed its response format and the types no longer match.

The hardest part isn't the tooling — it's the mindset shift. It means resisting the urge to quickly tweak a response field because it 'makes more sense.' It means adding a new endpoint instead of modifying an existing one when the shape needs to change. It means versioning your APIs not as an afterthought, but as a natural consequence of evolving contracts.

Looking back at projects like Chanakya, where legal predictions depend on precise data from multiple sources, or CodeLoom Explorer, where AST parsing relies on consistent compiler output formats, I realize that every robust system I've built had one thing in common: explicit, enforced contracts between its parts. The code quality mattered, but the contract discipline mattered more.
Code reviews will always have value. But if you want to ship software that doesn't break in production, start by reviewing your promises before you review your code.
